one_liner: Julia 0.6.3 ccall loop calling a trivial C function 1.3x faster than C's own PLT-routed call (2018 microbenchmark).
what_it_does: hello.jl calls plusone(int) from the repo's libnewplus.so 500 million times through ccall((:plusone, "./newplus/libnewplus.so"), Int32, (Cint,), x) and prints elapsed milliseconds; hello.c and hello.cpp run the same while (x < count) x = plusone(x) loop against the same shared library. It is a benchmark of foreign-call overhead, not a library: there is nothing to adopt except the observation that Julia's ccall to a constant (symbol, library) pair is a cheap native call with no marshalling for plain integer arguments.
how_it_is_fast: In Julia 0.6.3's codegen (src/ccall.cpp), a ccall whose library and symbol are constants is resolved with jl_dlsym_e at JIT time and the address is embedded as a literal pointer ('just JIT the function address'), so each iteration is one call through a constant pointer into plusone. The C and C++ executables are compiled with -fPIC and linked against libnewplus.so, so every call goes to the plusone@PLT stub and then jumps through the GOT: one extra branch per iteration on a loop whose body is only 'add 1 and return'. Both sides execute the same -O2 plusone machine code; the gap (1.78 vs 2.36 ns per call) is call-linkage overhead, not better code generation (mechanism from reading Tuprules.tup and Julia's ccall.cpp; the README states none).
when_to_use: As evidence that Julia's ccall into a C shared library adds essentially no overhead for scalar-argument functions, so wrapping a C library from Julia does not cost per-call time compared with C calling the same .so.

When deciding whether a hot loop of many tiny foreign calls belongs in Julia or C: on Julia 0.6-1.10 JIT-compiled code, a constant-library ccall is a direct pointer call, cheaper than C's default lazily bound PLT call.
As a reproducible harness (Tupfile, hello.*, run-all.sh) to measure call-boundary cost across about 20 languages on your own machine and toolchains.
when_not_to_use: As proof that Julia beats C in general: C calling plusone directly (static link, -fno-plt, LTO, or inlining) would remove the PLT hop, and issue #15 (open since 2019-12-16) asking for exactly that non-PLT C/C++ measurement was never answered.

On Julia 1.11 or later: current codegen no longer embeds the literal address in JIT mode; every non-vararg ccall with a constant library goes through emit_plt (a load from a per-symbol jlplt GOT slot, then an indirect call), which is structurally the same indirection as C's -fno-plt call, so the 2018 gap should not be assumed (not re-measured).
For functions that do real work: at 500M calls the whole difference is about 0.6 ns per call, which vanishes once the callee does more than a few instructions.
For calls that pass arrays, strings, structs or callbacks: only a single Cint argument and Int32 return were measured; marshalling costs are not covered.
As current data: toolchains are gcc 5.4.1, Julia 0.6.3 and LuaJIT 2.0.4 on a 2012 laptop CPU, with 2 samples per language; the repo's last commit is 2023-07-12.

integration.dependencies: Julia; the repo's newplus/libnewplus.so built with tup (gcc -O2 -fPIC -shared)
integration.min_toolchain: Julia 0.6.3 as measured (ccall tuple syntax still works in Julia 1.x); gcc 5.4.1 and tup 0.7.4 for the C side
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 as measured (Ubuntu 14.04, i7-3630QM); hello.jl hard-codes the relative path ./newplus/libnewplus.so

gotchas: Cross-run comparison: the C and C++ rows (1182/1182, 1182/1183 ms) are unchanged since the Feb 2017 README (commit 9f0c4d0), and the Julia row (894/889 ms) was added in May 2018 (commit c8010d5) without re-running C. The gap is still consistent with history: the 2013 run in prev.md (gcc 4.7.3, LuaJIT 2.0.2, 2 billion calls) already had LuaJIT at 3612 ms vs C 4839 ms, the same 1.34x ratio, and the 2018 Julia figure matches the 2017 LuaJIT figure (1.78 ns per call).

The C side is handicapped by its build, not by the language: Tuprules.tup puts -fPIC in CFLAGS for the executables too and links them against the shared library via rpath with default lazy binding, so the baseline is a PLT call; the Julia side gets a JIT-resolved constant pointer (Julia 0.6.3 ccall.cpp, non-imaging branch).

Version-specific mechanism: the literal-address path exists in Julia v0.6.3 through v1.10.0 ccall.cpp and is gone in v1.11.0 and current master, where use_jlplt defaults to 1 (src/init.c) and calls load the target from a jlplt GOT global; code compiled in imaging mode (system images) used the jlplt thunk in every version.

Timing differs slightly: C reads gettimeofday in whole milliseconds via current_timestamp() in the library, Julia uses time() as Float64 seconds; both exclude process start-up, and Julia's JIT compilation of run() happens before the timer starts.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The LuaJIT 2.0 FFI row in the same table shows the identical 1.3x gap (891/905 ms) for the same reason and was measured in the same 2017 run as C, so it is the cleaner citation; pick the Julia row only when the question is specifically Julia's ccall cost. Unlike the kostya and LangArena siblings, which compare whole algorithms, this measures only call linkage.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel i7-3630QM laptop under Ubuntu 14.04, 500 million calls of plusone() in a gcc -O2 -fPIC shared library took 894 and 889 ms from Julia 0.6.3 (2018 run) versus 1182 and 1182 ms from C and 1182/1183 ms from C++ built with gcc/g++ 5.4.1 -O2 (2017 run), about 1.3x faster (derived from page data). The difference is PLT indirection in the C executables versus a JIT-embedded function address in Julia.
status_note: Abandoned benchmark repo (last commit 2023-07-12, Apache-2.0, 698 stars) whose Julia number reflects a ccall code path that Julia removed in 1.11; usable only as a harness to re-measure call overhead, not as current evidence.
